figures.caption: Figure 1: Application classes of weakly-coupled wireless implantable BCI and relevant design constraints. a, Three application classes of today’s implantable wireless BCI: Open-loop high-density neural recording, Open-loop neuromodulation, and Closed-loop Bidirectional Brain Interface (BBI). b, current trends showing an exponential increase in the number of channels for neural interfaces. c, Uplink data rate limitations due to conventional high-energy communication, requiring lossy and power hungry compression at the node, which in turn increases system-level power consumption. More efficient communication can alleviate the bottleneck. d, Uplink power-vs-raw-data-rate landscape: today’s devices with ∼10,000-channels produce ∼1000 Mbps or more raw data. With a ∼10 mW uplink power budget, sub-10 pJ/b links are required, with a sub-1 pJ/b aspiration for million-channel raw streaming. e, Narrowband, high-Q resonant links for power and commands (FBW ∼0.1 to 1 %) versus wideband, low-Q links for high-rate data (FBW ∼80 %). To achieve the same bandwidth, wideband links require lower center frequencies, leading to lower link loss and lower power consumption.

Figure 2: Four-tier compute hierarchy: implant (P0), body-worn hub (P1), phone (or similar device - P2), cloud (P3) with a fast P0↔P1 local loop (≤10 ms) and a slow P0 → P3 deep loop. Latencies, powers and exemplar computations are shown for each tier, showing which computations are possible in which tiers.

Figure 3: Brain Implant Communication Technologies. a, weakly-coupled region definition. b, available techniques (tethered/untethered) for communication with a brain implant. c, description of popular techniques: ultrasonic, RF, inductive coupling, magneto-electric, brain channel communication, optical, backscatter and wired technologies in the current context.

Figure 4: Insights obtained from state-of-the-art wireless link implementations for Brain Implants. a, Data Rate vs. Depth shows that wideband techniques (such as UWB or BCC) achieves significantly higher data rates than narrowband techniques. However, narrowband US or ME techniques, due to their low loss, can support higher depth (3-5 cm) for future applications. BCC has also been explored for >5 cm depth, and has proven to achieve higher data rates than conventional narrowband. The numerical values near the data points indicate the data rate in Mbps. b, Energy-efficiency vs. Data Rate, which demonstrates the improved energy efficiencies of wideband techniques (UWB or BCC) over narrowband. Interestingly, some of the narrowband techniques (such as US or ME) hits a limit in terms of geometries, and prove to be insufficient to support higher carrier frequencies or data rates. The numerical values near the data points indicate the energy-efficiency in pJ/b. c, Depending on the application and the surgical needs, one modality can be preferred over others, which dictates the commercial adoption of the technology.
